1. Heard learned counsel for the petitioner and learned APP for the State.
2.

By the present petition, the petitioner seeks quashment of the order dated 22.10.2019 passed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge, Kandhar, District Nanded in Criminal Revision No. 41 of 2015, whereby the learned Sessions Judge affirmed the order dated 24.09.2015 passed by the learned Judicial Magistrate, First Class, Loha, District Nanded in Criminal OMCA No. 198 of 2015.

sentences.text:
By the said order, the application filed by the present petitioner under Section 156(3) of the Criminal Procedure Code, seeking directions to the concerned Police Station to investigate into the alleged preparation of false and fabricated revenue record, i.e. Village Form No. 7-B, in respect of land bearing Gat No. 48 of village Kiroda, Taluka Loha, District Nanded, came to be rejected by the learned JMFC, Loha.
2 of 6 45wp156-20 3.

The learned counsel appearing for the petitioner canvassed in vehemence that the petitioner filed an application bearing Criminal OMCA No. 198 of 2015 before the learned JMFC, Loha alleging that, he is owner and in possession of land bearing survey No. 48/5 admeasuring 80 R on the basis of registered Sale Deed dated 03.01.1981.
He has purchased the said land from Tukaram Dhondiba Mane.
The petitioner is also owner of another land admeasuring 34 R purchased from Tukaram Dhondiba Mane under sale dated 08.02.1984.
Accordingly, name of the petitioner is recorded in 7/12 extract in respect of the said land.

However, Respondent No.2 to 7, in collusion with Respondent Nos. 8 to 10, created false and fabricated revenue record i.e. 7/12 extract and Vilalge Form No. 7-B and shown Maroti Kondiba Mane/respondent No.2 is in possession of land bearing Gat No. 48/5.
Therefore, prayed for enquiry under section 156 Cr.P.C.
However, on 24.09.2015, the learned JMFC passed an order and rejected the prayer for investigation under section 156(3).

4. Learned counsel for the petitioner further canvassed that, as per the provisions of Section 415 of the Indian Penal Code, if any person dishonestly induces another person to deal with any property 3 of 6 45wp156-20 and prepares or uses a forged document by pretending it to be genuine, such person is said to have committed cheating.
Therefore, offence under section 415, 468, 470 IPC are made out.
However, both the courts below failed to consider the essential ingredients to constitute the offence under section 420, 447 and 471 read with section 34 IPC.
Hence prayed to quash and set aside the impugned orders.

5. Needless to say that, the petitioner claimed that the present respondent nos. 2 to 7, in collusion with respondent nos. 8, 9 and 10 have forged Revenue Record village Form No. 7-B and shown Maroti Kondiba Mane/respondent no.2 in possession as per Panchanama dated on 13.09.2013.

However, on the face of record, it appears that the present petitioner/informant has already initiated a proceeding under the Maharashtra Land Revenue Code, 1966 and prayed for correction of revenue record including village form 7-B, which is subject matter of the complaint.

Therefore,
once, the petitioner approached the competent authority under the MLRC for correction of the Revenue Record, further enquiry/investigation under section 156(3) Cr.P.C. is not required.
6. Further, the present respondent Nos. 8 to 10/original accused nos. 7 to 9 are public servant.
Therefore, for the prosecution of public servant, necessary sanction under section 197 Cr.P.C. is required.
However, the petitioner failed to bring on record that he has obtained such sanction for prosecution of the public servants i.e. present respondent nos. 8, 9 and 10 from the competent authority.
Therefore, 4 of 6 45wp156-20 in absence of such sanction, respondent nos. 8, 9 and 10 cannot be prosecuted.

7. On 24.09.2015, the learned JMFC, Loha passed an order and observed that as per the allegations of the present petitioner/ complainant, all the accused have prepared false documents to show possession of respondent no.2 in respect of agricultural land; however, there is not a single whisper about preparation of false documents by the accused persons in connivance with each other and the property was in possession of respondent no.2.

Therefore, the petitioner failed to bring the material on record to attract the ingredients of section 420, 447, 471 IPC.
8.

On 22.10.2019, the learned Revisional Court passed the impugned order upholding the order dated 24.09.2015 passed by the learned JMFC, Loha holding that, as per the allegations, respondent Nos. 2 to 7/ original accused nos. 1 to 6 in collusion with respondent no.8/ original accused no.7 have prepared false record and submitted a report on 27.01.2014 to respondent no.10(original accused no.9).
However, the complaint came to filed on 24.09.2015 i.e. after 7 months and 27 days.
So also, accused Nos. 1 to 9 (Respondent Nos. 2 to 10) have prepared false record i.e. Spot Panchanama and revenue record in respect of the subject land.

Respondent No.10- Tahsildar, the Revenue Authority, on the basis of false record, passed the order and in case the complainant has Vishveshwar S/O. Bhagwat Papinwar vs The State Of Maharashtra And Others on 4 March, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/178138828/
3 any grievance, he can avail proper remedy.

sentences.text: It further appears that Respondent No.2 has initiated the appropriate proceeding for correction of the Revenue Record before the Tahsildar.
Accordingly, the Revenue Authority passed an order showing the name of accused No. 1/respondent No. 2 in the cultivation column of 7/12 extract in respect of the land.
10. Section 257 of the Maharashtra Land Revenue Code, 1966 creates bar of jurisdiction of Civil Courts in certain matters relating to revenue authorities.

The said provision stipulates that no Civil Court shall have jurisdiction to decide or deal with any question which is required to be decided or dealt with by a revenue officer or any other authority under the Code.
Section 247 of the MLR Code provides about powers of Revenue Authorities as well Appeal, Revision, as stipulated under Schedule-E of the Code.
Therefore, a remedy is available to the petitioner before the competent authority under the Code to challenge the said order.
11. In view of above discussion, I do not find that the petitioner has made out any substantial ground to interfere with the findings recorded by both the Courts below.
The findings recorded by both the Courts appear to be just and proper.
Hence, the present petition deserves to be dismissed and accordingly, it is dismissed.
